text: I now give the floor to his excellency
Muhammad Hassan, Minister of
Foreign Affairs of Malaysia.
Mr. President, excellencies,
distinguished delegate, ladies and
gentlemen,
I join others in congratulating my
friend, his excellency Dr. Khalilu Raman
on his election as president of the 81st
session of the United Nation General
Assembly.
Dr. Mr. Kalu, you have Malaysia's full
support as you lead this assembly
through a period of profound global
uncertainty.
Mr. President, indeed we are meeting at
the most challenging time for the UN in
many years.
The world has become accustomed to
crisis.
War are escalating.
Major power rivalry is sharpening. The
international arm control architecture
is under strain. New technologies are
transforming societies faster than our
institution can adapt.
But perhaps the greatest danger is not
any one crisis. It is the growing belief
that the international system cannot
solve them. This is the trust deficit
confronting the UN today. And Malaysia,
Mr. President believes that we must
confront it openly and honestly.
Trust can only be restored through
concrete action when international law
means what it says and when the people
of the world can look to this hall and
believe that their word their voices
still matters. Mr. President, we must
remember that the UN is not merely here
for the aftermath of war, but to prevent
war from taking place.
Yet too often, we respond only after
disaster has arrived. We count the date,
we deliver supplies, we rebuild what has
been destroyed, and then we wait for the
next crisis.
This cannot be a future of
multilateralism.
We must move from reaction to
prevention.
And nowhere is that task more urgent
than in Gaza.
Mr. President, Malaysia will not stand
here and research statistics that
everyone in this hall already knows. We
all know the scale of death in Gaza. We
know how many children, families, medic,
aid workers and journalists have been
slaughtered.
We also know that Gaza represents the
highest number of children met orphans
in a single conflict. Malaysia and many
other member state have exhausted
the purs and every effort in pursuit of
justice for Gaza. We have consistently
called for immediate ceasefire
and unrestricted supply of aid. We have
supported im humanitarian works in
Palestine. We have pushed for punitive
actions towards Israel
and we have advocated for full
Palestinian membership in this hall. And
yet again and again, Mr. President, the
collective will of this assembly has
accounted the silencing effect of the
veto.
Malaysia, we speak plainly, Mr.
President. We are sick of it. Mr.
President, nowhere is the need for
reform more critical than in the
security council. Nowhere are the
shortcomings of the United Nation more
glaring than in the security council.
The exercise of veto must be questioned
and strongly challenged by every single
member of this general assembly
particularly in cases of crimes against
humanity.
Resolution 76 oblique 262
has already created an accountability
channel between the council and this
assembly.
We must we must make full use of this
resolution as a launch as a launchpad
for greater accountability regarding the
use of veto. Expanding the council's
membership alone will not be enough to
resolve its failure. It is the veto that
must be challenged and it is the veto
must be abolished. We must begin the
work now.
There is still time to save the global
order. The paralysis of security council
will not be the paralysis of United
Nation. Mr. President, it is fair to say
that global trust in the United Nation
ability to deliver is at all all-time
low.
This in turn demolishes trust in the
very idea of the multilateral order. The
citizens we serve and represent are
afraid. excellencies. They are watching
the world order fragment. They are
witnessing the reemergence of arm race.
They have heard over threat over use
nuclear weapons. And they are seeing
their government choose not to regulate
AI and the many ways it is being abused
but instead give it more power. In such
chaotic times, the only way to course
correct is to rebuild trust in the power
of proactive governance and
multilateralism.
Mr. President, trust comes from the way
in which we as the world leaders can
manage transformation forces. For
centuries, global power was constrated
in states. But today, a new source of
power have emerged. A handful of private
actors now control how billions of
people communicate, work, transact and
consume information.
Artificial intelligence is changing how
economies operate, how societies
function and how governments make
decisions. The opportunities are
enormous but also are the risks.
We must therefore ask simple question.
Who governs the transformation?
Technology must serve humanity, never
the reverse. And the answer cannot be
that small number of companies or
countries decide the rules for everyone
else.
The United Nation must continue to
empower global south countries who are
likely to be more greatly affected by
unequitable AI development to
participate in global discussion or on
AI.
The global south cannot simply become a
destination of for data centers while
decisions about AI are made elsewhere.
We must be partners in innovation, not
merely customers and market and not
merely destinations for investment.
Partners involved in the decisions that
will shape our future. Equitable
decision making and equitable
development. That means managing the
enormous demands that tech
infrastructure places on water, energy,
land and other resources that so that
the benefits of AI can be shared more
broadly across the borders.
Mr. President, in our hyperconnected
world today, indeed very few things
stays where they begin. Technologies are
rapidly shared and they can just as
rapidly disrupt. Similarly, war can also
travel beyond borders. Across West Asia,
escalating conflict threatens some of
the world's most important routes for
energy and trade, including the street
of Homos and the B al- Mahad al- Mad.
The consequences of conflict do not stop
at this source. A family in Southeast
Asia has no part in this disputes. Yet
that family still pays the price when
food, fuel, and cost of living rise.
Malaysia therefore urges all parties to
step back from escalation. Diplomacy has
shown that dialogue is possible, that
path must not be abandoned,
or we risk sending further shock waves
through global markets and needlessly
bringing suffering to innocent families
around the world. Mr. President,
most nations in this hall are not great
powers. Yet decision taken by few can
shape the future for all.
We are the global majority. As I said
earlier, we must not simply live with
the consequences of choices made
elsewhere. We must help shape those
choices.
Middle powers such as Malaysia can help
keep dialogue alive when major powers
cannot agree. regional organization
such as ASEAN can bring the perspectives
to their pe of their people into global
debates. We must have the confidence of
to speak for our regions not be spoken
for. Mr. President, I began by speaking
about trust. Let me close where I began.
The question before us may appear
simple, but in truth it is profound.
When people are suffering and when the
world looks towards this hall, will this
organization still answer the call for
which it was created?
Actions speak louder than words. My
esteem colleagues, we must restore
trust, manage transformation,
reform institution that no longer serve
current realities.
And we must ensure that the rules of the
global system apply equally to all.
Malaysia will not turn away from the UN
in its hour of difficulty. We will not
abandon multilateralism
just because it it is imperfect. We will
do the work to make it worthy of the
trust placed in it because we believe in
multilateralism
most of all when the alternative is a
world rule by power alone. Excellencies,
80 years ago the founders of this
organization resolve to save succeeding
generations from war. We are those
succeeding generation and that promise
now rests in our hand. The world needs a
UN that delivers, one that ensures that
international law is truly international
and guarantees that every region has a
voice and above all one that ordinary
people can look to in their darkest hour
and still believe that ill will act that
the world has not forgotten. and
excellencies before concluding
we would like to offer our most
heartfelt gratitude to the secretary
general Antonio Gutes
as this will the final session of the
general assembly during his tenure. We
thank him for leading the UN with
unyielding dedication and patience
through many unprecedented global
upheavalss.
These are the qualities we will need to
face our future as an organization.
And if there is anything that humanity
has demonstrated throughout our history,
it is our capacity to adapt. My esteemed
colleague, Mr. President Sences, let us
adapt and prove ourself worthy of the
promise and trusted us.
Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank uh I thank the Minister of
Foreign Affairs of Malaysia.
